subject: Endocrine
vignette: An 18-year-old lean student presents with polydipsia, polyuria, polyphagia, and weight loss and is found to have ketoacidosis. Testing is positive for islet cell cytoplasmic antibodies and glutamic acid decarboxylase antibodies.
question: Which of the following best describes the primary defect in this patient's disease?

options.text: Increased insulin resistance with progressive pancreatic beta-cell failure
A monogenic defect in the insulin receptor
Excessive glucagon secretion from pancreatic alpha cells
Autoimmune T-cell-mediated destruction of pancreatic beta cells
Glucocorticoid-induced insulin resistance

explanation_correct: This is type 1 diabetes, caused by autoimmune T-cell-mediated destruction of pancreatic beta cells; islet cell cytoplasmic, GAD, and insulin autoantibodies are often present. It produces absolute insulin deficiency, severe glucose intolerance, high insulin sensitivity, and common ketoacidosis, and requires insulin always. HLA-DR4 and -DR3 are associated (4 minus 3 = type 1).

explanation_incorrect.A: Insulin resistance with progressive beta-cell failure is the primary defect of type 2 diabetes, not type 1.
explanation_incorrect.B: A monogenic insulin receptor defect is a rare form of severe insulin resistance, not autoimmune type 1 diabetes.
explanation_incorrect.C: Excess glucagon is not the primary defect of type 1 diabetes; the core problem is beta-cell destruction.
explanation_incorrect.E: Glucocorticoid-induced insulin resistance is steroid diabetes, not autoimmune beta-cell destruction.

educationalObjective: Type 1 DM results from autoimmune T-cell beta-cell destruction with autoantibodies and absolute insulin deficiency.
source: Generated from 8. Endocrine.pdf - Pathology: Type 1 vs type 2 diabetes mellitus

subject: Endocrine
vignette: A 55-year-old obese man is diagnosed with diabetes. He has a strong family history, mild glucose intolerance, no ketoacidosis, and does not require insulin.
question: Which histologic finding is most consistent with this patient's disease?

options.text: Islet leukocytic infiltrate
Islet amyloid polypeptide deposits
Complete absence of islets with fibrosis
Islet beta-cell hyperplasia
Calcification of the pancreatic islets

explanation_correct: Type 2 diabetes is characterized by islet amyloid polypeptide deposits. Its primary defect is insulin resistance with progressive beta-cell failure; beta-cell numbers are variable, serum insulin is elevated initially and falls in advanced disease, and ketoacidosis is rare. It is associated with obesity and a strong genetic predisposition but no HLA association.

explanation_incorrect.A: Islet leukocytic infiltrate (insulitis) is the histologic hallmark of autoimmune type 1 diabetes.
explanation_incorrect.C: Complete absence of islets with fibrosis is not typical; type 2 has variable beta-cell numbers with amyloid deposits.
explanation_incorrect.D: Beta-cell hyperplasia is not the characteristic histology of type 2 diabetes; amyloid deposition is.
explanation_incorrect.E: Islet calcification is not a feature of type 2 diabetes.

educationalObjective: Type 2 DM shows islet amyloid polypeptide deposits, insulin resistance, and variable beta-cell numbers.

subject: Endocrine
vignette: A 68-year-old man with obesity and long-standing type 2 diabetes has required insulin for several years. Early in his disease serum insulin was elevated; currently it is low.
question: Which of the following best explains the decline in his serum insulin?

options.text: Autoimmune destruction of beta cells developing later in life
Appearance of islet cell and GAD autoantibodies
HLA-DR3/DR4-mediated beta-cell destruction
A marked decrease in insulin resistance alone
Progressive pancreatic beta-cell failure after initial compensatory hyperinsulinemia in type 2 diabetes

explanation_correct: In type 2 diabetes the primary defect is insulin resistance; early on, beta cells compensate by increasing insulin secretion (hyperinsulinemia). Over time progressive beta-cell failure develops, so serum insulin eventually falls in advanced disease — this is distinct from autoimmune type 1 diabetes. Beta-cell numbers are variable with amyloid deposits, and ketoacidosis remains rare.

explanation_incorrect.A: New autoimmune beta-cell destruction would convert the patient to type 1, which is not the typical course of long-standing type 2 disease.
explanation_incorrect.B: Islet cell and GAD autoantibodies are markers of type 1 diabetes, not the expected explanation for type 2 beta-cell decline.
explanation_incorrect.C: HLA-DR3/DR4 association belongs to type 1 diabetes; type 2 has no HLA association.
explanation_incorrect.D: Reduced insulin resistance would lower insulin demand but would not cause the loss of beta-cell secretory capacity described.

educationalObjective: Serum insulin in type 2 DM is initially elevated but falls with progressive beta-cell failure in advanced disease.

subject: Endocrine
vignette: A 52-year-old obese patient is newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes.
question: Compared with a patient with type 1 diabetes, which of the following is most likely characteristic of this patient's disease?

options.text: Low insulin sensitivity with initially elevated serum insulin
High insulin sensitivity with low serum insulin
High insulin sensitivity with high serum insulin
Low insulin sensitivity with low serum insulin from the outset
Normal insulin sensitivity with absolute insulin deficiency

explanation_correct: Type 2 diabetes features low insulin sensitivity (insulin resistance) and serum insulin that is elevated initially before falling in advanced disease. In contrast, type 1 diabetes has high insulin sensitivity and low serum insulin from autoimmune beta-cell destruction. Other type 2 features include obesity, strong genetic predisposition (90% twin concordance), mild-to-moderate glucose intolerance, and rare ketoacidosis.

explanation_incorrect.B: High insulin sensitivity with low serum insulin is characteristic of type 1 diabetes.
explanation_incorrect.C: Type 2 diabetes has low, not high, insulin sensitivity.
explanation_incorrect.D: In type 2 diabetes serum insulin is initially elevated, not low from the outset.
explanation_incorrect.E: Normal insulin sensitivity with absolute insulin deficiency describes type 1, not type 2.

educationalObjective: Type 2 DM: low insulin sensitivity with initially high serum insulin; type 1 DM: high sensitivity with low insulin.

subject: Endocrine
vignette: A researcher compares the genetic and immunologic features of type 1 and type 2 diabetes mellitus.
question: Which of the following statements about these two diseases is correct?

options.text: Type 2 diabetes has 50% concordance in identical twins and is associated with HLA-DR3/DR4
Type 1 diabetes has 90% concordance in identical twins and no HLA association
Type 1 diabetes is associated with HLA-DR4/DR3 and has about 50% twin concordance, whereas type 2 has about 90% concordance and no HLA association
Both type 1 and type 2 diabetes show a strong HLA-DR4 association
Type 2 diabetes has a weak genetic predisposition with 50% concordance in identical twins

explanation_correct: Type 1 diabetes has a relatively weak genetic predisposition (about 50% concordance in identical twins) and is associated with HLA-DR4 and -DR3 ('4 minus 3 = type 1'). Type 2 diabetes has a relatively strong genetic predisposition (about 90% twin concordance) and no HLA association. This contrast is a high-yield discriminator between the two diseases.

explanation_incorrect.A: Both the 50% concordance and the HLA-DR3/DR4 association belong to type 1 diabetes, not type 2.
explanation_incorrect.B: Type 1 has about 50% (not 90%) concordance and does have HLA associations; it is type 2 that has 90% concordance.
explanation_incorrect.D: HLA-DR4 is associated only with type 1 diabetes; type 2 has no HLA association.
explanation_incorrect.E: Type 2 has a strong (not weak) genetic predisposition with about 90% concordance; weak/50% belongs to type 1.

educationalObjective: Type 1 DM: weak genetic (50% concordance), HLA-DR3/DR4; type 2 DM: strong genetic (90% concordance), no HLA association.
